8.03.t: Talus Blood Supply — the Real Question
8.03.b:
### The arteries
| Artery | From | Enters | Supplies |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Artery of the tarsal canal** | Posterior tibial | Tarsal canal, from medial | **Main supply of the body** (Gelberman 1983)  |
[[FIG: Fig 8.6 · 8.03
| **Deltoid branch** | Artery of the tarsal canal | Through the deep deltoid | **Medial body** → saved if the deltoid is kept |
| **Artery of the sinus tarsi** | Peroneal perforating + dorsalis pedis | Sinus tarsi, from lateral | Neck and lateral body |
| **Superomedial / dorsal neck branches** | Dorsalis pedis | Dorsal neck | **Head and neck** |
| Posterior tubercle branches | Peroneal + posterior tibial | Posterior process | Small part of the body |

- Canal + sinus arteries → **sling under the neck**; flow **retrograde** → a neck fracture kills the body, the head survives (Netter)
- Share by MRI → **PT (posterior tibial) 47% · anterior tibial 36% · peroneal 17%** (Miller 2011)
- New **medial neck branch** → cut by a standard anteromedial approach (Prasarn 2010)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "Blood supply of the talus"
- No muscle, 60% cartilage → vessels enter at **neck, sinus tarsi, tarsal canal, medial body, posterior process**
- Main → **artery of the tarsal canal** (posterior tibial) → body; its **deltoid branch** → medial body
- **Artery of the sinus tarsi** (peroneal + dorsalis pedis) → lateral body; **dorsalis pedis** → head and neck
- Canal + sinus form a **sling under the neck** → retrograde flow → a neck fracture threatens the body
- Hawkins I → IV → AVN (avascular necrosis) **10% → 100%** (table below) · **Hawkins sign** = alive (Netter)

| Hawkins type | What is displaced | AVN (Netter) |
|---|---|---|
| I | Undisplaced neck | 10% |
| II | + subtalar dislocation | 40% |
| III | + ankle (tibiotalar) dislocation | 90% |
| IV | + talonavicular dislocation | 100% |

[[FIG: Fig 8.7 · 8.03

- **Hawkins sign** → subchondral lucency at 6–8 weeks = revascularised body, no AVN (Netter)

EXAM PEARL — why not every neck fracture dies
- Rich intraosseous anastomosis + **posterior entry** of PT vessels → many bodies survive (Miller 2011)

- Talar neck exposure → **dual approach**, never strip the deltoid (Prasarn 2010) → 8B

8.06.b:
### The mortise
- **Hinge** → **DF (dorsiflexion) 20°, PF (plantar flexion) 50°** (Netter) · load ≈5× body weight in walking (OB Foot)
  [[FIG: Fig 8.23 · 8.06
- Mortise → plafond above, medial malleolus, lateral malleolus; **only the talus** of the tarsals enters it (Bontrager)
- DF → the fibula **rotates and widens** the mortise round the wide front of the talus (OB Foot)
- So → **cast in neutral, never in plantar flexion** → the narrow back of the talus sags (Handbook)

### Syndesmosis — four ligaments
| Ligament | Runs | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **AITFL** | Chaput tubercle → anterior fibula | Oblique, 3 bands; **torn first** in external rotation (Bartoníček 2003) |
| **PITFL** | Posterior malleolus → posterior fibula | Strong; avulses the **Volkmann** fragment instead of tearing |
| **ITL** (inferior transverse) | Deep part of the PITFL | **Labrum** of the posterior plafond (Bartoníček 2003) |
| **IOL** (interosseous) | Lowest thickening of the IOM (interosseous membrane) | Pyramid of fibres + fat |
